regimes.name: US tax resident (citizen, green card holder or substantial presence)
regimes.description: Worldwide taxation at federal level; state income and estate taxes come on top depending on the state of residence.
regimes.eligibility: Citizens are always taxed; non-citizens are resident with a green card or under the substantial presence test (183 weighted days over 3 years, at least 31 in the current year). Non-citizens need an immigrant or long-stay visa (e.g. EB-5, E-2, L-1).

capital_gains.summary: Combined federal + New York top rate on a large long-term gain: 34.7% (federal 20% + 3.8% NIIT + state 10.9%). New York State top rate 10.9% (above USD 25 million); gains and dividends are ordinary income. Residents of New York City add the city's personal income tax (top 3.876%), giving 14.776% state+city, i.e. a combined top rate of 38.576% with the federal 23.8%. The rates here are state-only; NYC is described separately. Top marginal state rate per Tax Foundation 2026 table.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Federal: 20% bracket above USD 613,700 taxable income (MFJ, 2026); NIIT above USD 250,000 MAGI (MFJ). State: top rate reached at the thresholds stated in the summary.
capital_gains.regional_differences: New York City residents: +3.876% (top) on the same base, so combined 38.576% on gains and qualified dividends. Yonkers residents: surcharge of 16.75% of state tax. These local taxes are not included in the rates.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: State income tax is effectively not deductible federally for a top-bracket family (SALT cap; itemized deductions limited), so state and federal rates are simply added. Most states do not give a credit for foreign taxes paid. Unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real estate is taxed federally at 25% + 3.8%.

inheritance.summary: New York estate tax: basic exclusion USD 7,350,000 for 2026 deaths, rates 3.06%-16% (Tax Law 952). Cliff: the credit phases out between 100% and 105% of the exclusion, so an estate above USD 7,717,500 is taxed on its WHOLE value from the first dollar. The JSON therefore uses exemption 0 and the full rate table, which is exact for taxable estates above USD 7,717,500; estates up to USD 7.35 million pay nothing. Gifts made within three years of death are added back. Combined with the federal estate tax (40% above USD 15,000,000; state death taxes are deductible federally under IRC 2058), the brackets are the combined marginal rates for an estate passing entirely to children: federal tax starts once the estate net of state tax exceeds USD 15 million (about USD 17.22 million gross). Illustrative combined tax for an unmarried decedent: 18.0% of a USD 20 million estate, 37.0% of USD 50 million. Federal portability (married couple, USD 30M combined exclusion) applied on 2026-10-15: the federal 40% now starts at a gross estate of about USD 35.08 million.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: State exemption used: USD 0 (per estate); federal basic exclusion USD 15,000,000 per person (2026), portable between spouses (state exemptions generally are NOT portable, except as noted).
inheritance.important_exceptions: Unlimited marital deduction at both levels for a US-citizen spouse; the state tax usually becomes due at the second death. Most states' exemptions are not portable, so couples use credit-shelter trusts. Bracket list is a best-faith combination of two different tax structures (see summary); it assumes no lifetime gifts, a single decedent, no other deductions.

inheritance.gift_tax: No state gift tax; lifetime gifts escape the state estate tax (subject to any add-back noted in the summary). Federal gift tax is unified with the federal estate tax (40% after the USD 15M lifetime exclusion).
inheritance.business_relief: Federal: no exemption, IRC 6166 deferral. State-level relief for family farms and small businesses exists in several states (e.g. Minnesota qualified small business/farm deduction, Maryland family farm) but never covers a listed portfolio.
inheritance.foreign_assets: Residents (domiciliaries) are taxed on worldwide intangibles; real and tangible property located in another state or abroad is generally excluded or apportioned at state level.
inheritance.domicile_rules: State death taxes follow domicile at death (intention to remain, home, voting, driver's licence, time spent). A move must be complete before death; states audit claimed changes of domicile. Non-domiciliaries pay only on in-state real and tangible property.

regimes.name: Irrevocable GST-exempt dynasty trust taxed as a grantor trust
regimes.description: The parents each give up to their USD 15 million gift/estate exclusion (USD 30 million for a couple) to an irrevocable trust for the children and later generations, allocating the equal GST exemption so the trust is never subject to estate or generation-skipping tax. The trust is drafted as a grantor trust (e.g. a power to swap assets), so the parents keep paying the income tax on its gains and dividends at their own rates; those payments shrink their taxable estate without counting as further gifts. Assets in the trust and all their later growth pass outside the parents' taxable estates. Federal layer only; state income and estate taxes are not reflected in this regime.
regimes.eligibility: Donors must be US citizens or US-domiciled non-citizens to use the USD 15 million exclusion (non-domiciled non-citizens have no lifetime gift exclusion). The parents must give up control and benefit: they cannot be beneficiaries (except a spouse in a spousal lifetime access trust) or hold powers that pull the assets back into their estates (IRC 2036/2038). Perpetual duration requires a trust governed by the law of a state that has abolished or extended the rule against perpetuities (e.g. South Dakota, Nevada, Delaware). Gift-splitting needs both spouses to be citizens or residents.
regimes.duration_note: No federal time limit: the GST exemption allocated when the trust is funded protects the trust permanently, and in states without a rule against perpetuities the trust can last indefinitely. Grantor-trust status ends at the grantor's death or when the power is released; the trust then pays its own income tax (see exit_and_liquidation).

structure.entity: Irrevocable dynasty trust (intentionally defective grantor trust), usually a directed trust sitused in a no-perpetuities state
structure.payout_notes: Distributions of trust capital or income to the children are not taxable to them while the trust is a grantor trust: the parents already pay the tax on all trust income (IRC 671 ff.). The parents themselves cannot receive distributions without bringing the assets back into their estates, so the family's own spending must come from assets kept outside the trust (a spousal lifetime access trust lets one spouse benefit, at the cost of using only the other spouse's exclusion). After grantor status ends, a non-grantor trust is taxed at trust rates (ordinary income at 37% above USD 16,000 and long-term gains at 20% above USD 16,250 in 2026, Rev. Proc. 2025-32, plus 3.8% NIIT) unless it distributes income, which is then taxed to the beneficiaries.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: Running cost is a rough estimate (administrative or directed trustee fee, trust accounting and information returns, legal review), not sourced; investment management is assumed to stay with the family office. Grantor-trust rules: IRC 671-679 (a substitution power under IRC 675(4)(C) is the usual trigger). Estate inclusion risks: retained interests or control (IRC 2036, 2038), the reciprocal-trust doctrine for mirror-image spousal trusts, and implied agreements to benefit the grantor. The grantor's payment of the trust's income tax is not treated as a gift (Rev. Rul. 2004-64; not opened in this session). Trust assets get no step-up in basis at the grantor's death (Rev. Rul. 2023-2), so the children inherit the parents' cost basis and pay up to 23.8% when they sell, unless low-basis assets are swapped back to the grantor before death. State law matters: the trust's situs state determines perpetual duration and whether a non-grantor trust pays state income tax; Connecticut has a gift tax and some estate-tax states (e.g. New York) add back recent gifts. C-corporation alternatives are penalised: a personal holding company tax of 20% on undistributed passive income (IRC 541-542) and a 20% accumulated earnings tax (IRC 531) apply on top of 21% CIT.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: Emigration of the grantor: a covered expatriate faces the IRC 877A mark-to-market exit tax on assets he or she is treated as owning (grantor-trust assets included, per the IRS expatriation rules; not verified in detail), and later distributions to US beneficiaries of covered gifts can be hit by IRC 2801. Moving the trust's trustee or control abroad makes it a foreign trust and can trigger tax on unrealised gains (IRC 684; not verified). Terminating or distributing the trust is not an estate-tax event once GST exemption covers it; distributed assets keep their carryover basis.

residency.tax_residency_test: Income tax: citizens always; non-citizens with a green card (lawful permanent residents) or meeting the substantial presence test (at least 31 days in the year and 183 days counting all current-year days, 1/3 of prior-year days and 1/6 of the second prior year), subject to the closer-connection exception. Estate tax: domicile. Leaving after holding a green card in 8 of the last 15 years (long-term resident) or renouncing citizenship triggers the IRC 877A exit tax for covered expatriates (net worth USD 2 million or more, average net income tax above USD 211,000 for 2026, or failure to certify compliance).

income_tax.summary: US federal income tax only: 10% to 37% (2026 single brackets; standard deduction USD 16,100, modelled as the personal allowance). Austin, Texas adds no personal income tax: Texas has no state income tax and no local income tax was found for Austin. About 22% federal marginal rate at the 150,000 level. Employees pay 6.2% social security up to USD 184,500 plus 1.45% Medicare (plus 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages above USD 200,000, not modelled); the self-employed pay 15.3% (12.4% + 2.9%) on 92.35% of net earnings. Other states vary widely: nine have no wage income tax (for example Texas and Florida).
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Self-employment tax is 15.3% (12.4% social security + 2.9% Medicare) applied to 92.35% of net self-employment earnings (IRS Schedule SE line 4a/5b, opened 2026-10-15), so the rate on net earnings is 15.3% x 0.9235 = 14.13%. The 12.4% part stops at the wage base (USD 184,500 for 2026, i.e. net earnings of about USD 199,783 after the 92.35% factor); the cap field uses that point, but the 2.9% Medicare part is uncapped and a 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax applies above USD 200,000 (single; IRS), neither modelled above the cap. Half of the SE tax is deductible in computing income tax (IRS), not modelled. Self-employed people may deduct the employer-equivalent half of self-employment tax (IRS, in adjusted gross income), so about 0.5 of their contributions reduce taxable income; the employee figure (0) governs the field.
income_tax.local_tax_note: Brackets are the 2026 US federal schedule for a single filer on TAXABLE income (IRS release), applied after the USD 16,100 standard deduction (field personal_allowance). Texas levies no state income tax (Texas Comptroller) and no Austin local income tax was found; the previous New York State and New York City layers were removed. Not modelled: the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages above USD 200,000 (employer withholding, single filer), the Net Investment Income Tax, itemised deductions, the QBI deduction, and FICA non-deductibility (social_security_deductible 0). Texas property tax and sales tax are not income taxes and are outside this field.

income.residence_routes: There is no digital nomad visa. EU and many other nationals can visit on ESTA or B-1/B-2 status but may not work for US clients while there, so a remote worker has no direct immigration route; long stays need a work visa (H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN for Canada/Mexico), an investor visa or family sponsorship, all employer- or relationship-based. US citizens need no immigration route but owe US tax on worldwide income wherever they live. A skilled employee at a US employer typically uses H-1B (annual lottery), L-1 intra-company transfer or O-1.
open_questions: No nomad visa or special regime exists; covers_local_work does not apply.
